--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -1 +1,158 @@
-# ehl-zurich-2026
\ No newline at end of file
+# Open Relief
+
+Predict district-level **FEWS NET IPC phase three months ahead** from six months of
+monthly food-security, shipping, conflict, rainfall and food-price histories. Deterioration
+(an increase of at least one IPC phase) is a secondary analysis. Official OpenTSLM is the
+primary model; simple classical models are comparison baselines.
+
+Local data preparation and native TimeNet connectors are implemented. Annotation has been
+tested with a small live pilot; **full annotation runs later on this machine**, followed
+by fine-tuning on a separate CUDA machine. See [current status](docs/STATUS.md) for measured
+results and remaining work. No OpenTSLM improvement has been measured yet.
+
+## Current dataset
+
+| Partition | Rule | Examples |
+|---|---|---:|
+| Training | Target plus assumed release lag available by December 2022 | 9,065 |
+| Validation | January–July 2023 cutoffs, labels available by July 2023 | 2,503 |
+| Test | August–December 2023 cutoffs, exact target at cutoff +3 months | 2,230 |
+
+Labels that cross the training or validation freeze are purged. The eligible validation
+cutoffs therefore end in March 2023. Training spans 16 countries; test has 14, with no
+eligible Yemen or Ethiopia examples. These are country-imbalanced retrospective samples,
+not independent crisis events. Six complete monthly FCS/rCSI observations remain required.
+
+There are **21 monthly channels**, with an availability mask for each at model input:
+
+- FCS/rCSI normalized indices, and the requested plain `month_of_year` integers 1–12.
+- Last known IPC phase and assessment age, reconstructed as of each historical month.
+- Four PortWatch measures, ACLED events/fatalities, CHIRPS rainfall, WFP staple price.
+- One- and three-month price percentage changes and FCS/rCSI differences, trailing
+  three-month conflict events, and cargo imports relative to the previous three months.
+
+Derived series use only the existing six-point window. Early entries without enough
+history remain null, as do ratios with nonpositive denominators. No new downloads were
+needed for these features. Source prefixes are retained so an ablation removes both a
+source and its derived features. IPC history expires after six months without an assessment.
+
+All non-calendar series are scaled to [-1,1] within each input window, with original scale
+statistics and units retained in text. Calendar scaling is fixed from 1–12; there are no
+sine/cosine channels. The official patch-size-4 collator pads six observations to eight
+positions. Padding is a model operation, not extra observed months.
+

265	## 4. OpenTSLM (arXiv 2510.02410v3)
266	
267	Repo: `github.com/OpenTSLM/OpenTSLM` (redirects from `StanfordBDHG/OpenTSLM`).
268	
269	### 4.1 Architectures
270	
271	- **OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt** — learnable time-series tokens concatenated with text tokens.
272	  VRAM scales with both series count and series length; paper reports OOM for large inputs.
273	- **OpenTSLM-Flamingo** — time series as a separate modality via cross-attention.
274	  VRAM mostly bound by the LLM backbone.
275	
276	### 4.2 Sample structure (from source)
277	
278	`QADataset._format_sample` builds:
279	
280	```
281	PromptWithAnswer(
282	    TextPrompt(pre_prompt),                        # task instructions + label set
283	    [TextTimeSeriesPrompt(text, series), ...],     # one per 1-D channel
284	    TextPrompt(post_prompt),                       # e.g. "Rationale:"
285	    answer                                         # "<rationale> Answer: <label>"
286	)
287	```
288	
289	`TextTimeSeriesPrompt` asserts the series is 1-dimensional, non-empty, numeric.
290	Subclasses implement `_load_splits`, `_get_answer`, `_get_pre_prompt`, `_get_post_prompt`,
291	`_get_text_time_series_prompt_list`. Reference implementation: `HARCoTQADataset`.
292	
293	Series are rendered into the text prompt as:
294	`"The following is <description>, it has mean X and std Y:\n<values>"`
295	
296	### 4.3 CoT dataset generation method (§A.2)
297	
298	- Generator: **GPT-4o**, snapshot `gpt-4o-2024-08-06`, **temperature 0.3, seed 42**
299	- Input to generator: a **plot** of the series plus the **ground-truth label**
300	- The generator is shown **two** candidate labels — the correct one and a deliberately
301	  **dissimilar** distractor. At training and inference time the model is instead shown the
302	  **full** label set.
303	- Data plotted without normalization; multiple series rendered as subplots in one figure
304	- Prompt rules used verbatim:
305	  - analyze without assuming a specific label
306	  - think step-by-step
307	  - single natural paragraph, no bullets/numbered steps/headings
308	  - do not refer to the plot or to visual analysis
309	  - do not mention any class label until the final sentence
310	  - must end with `Answer: [CORRECT_LABEL]`
311	- QC: prompt engineering plus manual review of a subset
312	- Splits: 80/10/10 for all datasets
313	
314	### 4.4 Dataset sizes (Table 4)
315	
316	| Dataset | Train / Val / Test | Series | Length |
317	|---|---|---|---|
318	| TSQA | 38,400 / 4,800 / 4,800 | 1 | — |
319	| M4-Captions | 80,000 / 10,000 / 10,000 | 1 | 64–512 pts |
320	| HAR-CoT | 68,542 / 8,718 / 8,222 | 3 | 2.56 s @ 50 Hz |
321	| Sleep-CoT | 7,434 / 930 / 930 | 1 | 30 s @ 100 Hz |
322	| ECG-QA-CoT | 159,313 / 31,137 / 41,093 | 12 | 10 s @ 100 Hz |
323	
324	### 4.5 Training configuration (§A.1.1)
325	
326	AdamW · encoder LR 2e-4 · LoRA 2e-4 · cross-attention 2e-4 · projector 1e-4 ·
327	linear schedule with 10% warmup · gradient clipping ℓ2 = 1.0 · weight decay 0.01 ·
328	up to 200 epochs, early stopping patience 5.
329	
330	### 4.6 Reported results (macro-F1)
331	
332	| Task | OpenTSLM best | GPT-4o baseline |
333	|---|---|---|
334	| TSQA | 84.54 (82.06 acc) | 45.32 |
335	| HAR-CoT | 65.44 | 2.95 |
336	| Sleep-CoT | 54.40 (72.04 acc) | 15.47 |
337	| ECG-QA-CoT | 40.25 | 18.19 |
338	
339	### 4.7 Limitations stated by the authors
340	
341	- CoT datasets were generated by GPT-4o from plots, and GPT-4o performs poorly on those
342	  plots alone; the paper states curated datasets would likely yield better rationales.
343	- The model can produce a correct rationale with an incorrect final answer; the loss does
344	  not explicitly enforce answer correctness.
345	- SoftPrompt VRAM grows with series count and length, becoming impractical for long inputs.
346	- ECG-QA fine-tuning of tokenized baselines was infeasible at their sequence lengths.

350	## 5. Structural properties relevant to modelling
351	
352	Stated as properties of the data, not as recommendations.
353	
354	1. `ipc_phase_fews` is published on a 3–4 month cycle; `fcs_rt`/`rcsi_rt` are monthly. A
355	   monthly IPC input channel is not constructible from this file.
356	2. `hfid_hv1.csv` carries admin unit **names only, no P-codes**. ACLED (via HDX) carries
357	   P-codes. Joining the two requires either name matching or an external boundary set.
358	   The `ALL_HFIC` shapefiles cannot supply boundaries — they are dissolved by phase.
359	3. PortWatch port values are **country-level**: identical for every district within a
360	   country in a given month. PortWatch chokepoint values are **global**: identical for
361	   every district worldwide in a given month.
362	4. Port import volumes differ by orders of magnitude between countries (Nigeria 1,088,848 t
363	   vs. Somalia 87,375 t monthly mean) and carry seasonality.
364	5. `import_dry_bulk` includes non-food commodities (coal, ore, fertilizer, cement).
365	6. Phase 5 does not occur in any usable window. Phase 4 occurs in 332 of 15,593 (2.1%).
366	7. The five largest countries by sample count (Yemen, Nigeria, Kenya, Guatemala, Malawi)
367	   account for 74% of district samples.
368	8. District windows overlap in time within an admin unit; a random split places overlapping
369	   windows from the same unit in different partitions.
370	9. Sample counts in §2.2 require only `fcs_rt`/`rcsi_rt` completeness. Any additional
371	   channel made mandatory intersects this set downward.
372	10. Rainfall affects food security at harvest, on a lag tied to the growing-season calendar,
373	    which varies by country. FEWS NET publishes per-country seasonal calendars.

# Open Relief status — 12 September 2026

**Local preparation is implemented. Full annotation is deliberately deferred until later
on this machine; GPU training and the OpenTSLM before/after comparison remain pending.**

## Dataset and added features

Final dataset version:
`8142c89de89cb862117d6a814be515b9f00312bb960e33cf7e994a99ed124bd3`.

- Primary target: district FEWS IPC phase at cutoff +3 months; secondary deterioration:
  at least one phase increase over the latest available assessment, no older than six months.
- Six monthly history points; month of year remains a single integer 1–12 series.
- Training: 9,065 examples across 16 countries. Validation: 2,503 across 16. Test: 2,230
  across 14. No eligible Yemen or Ethiopia test examples under the selected dates.
- Added ten channels without additional downloads: monthly known IPC and assessment age;
  price changes at one/three months; FCS/rCSI differences at one/three months; trailing
  three-month conflict events; cargo imports versus their prior three-month mean.
- Total: 21 channels plus observation masks. Changes retain their source prefix for ablations.
- Rebuilt price selection excludes milling services and matches actual staple commodities.
  Yemen's selected series is imported rice, with exact package unit retained.

Checksums, temporal splits, input availability, channel shapes, calendar values and
annotation alignment are checked by `open_relief.validate`. See
[the current validation report](../reports/dataset-validation.json).
Missing covariates and initial rolling-window entries remain null, not zero observations.
Price coverage is 73%, shipping 79%, conflict 100%, rainfall 83% after assumed lag masking.

## Annotation pipeline

The final local suite passes 19 tests, including temporal leakage, derived-feature missingness,
IPC assessment chronology, budget accounting and native TimeF serialization.

Six-example live pilots use `gpt-5.6-terra` and the official OpenAI API. The final selection
covers six countries and includes improvement, deterioration and stable outcomes. JSON
schema validation and exact objective-label preservation pass. Full training annotations
have **not** been generated. The final pilot output and request usage are in
`artifacts/annotations-final-pilot.jsonl` and its adjacent manifest.

Manual review identified a confusion between the age of a rolling IPC record and the
newer assessment available at the forecast cutoff. The request now explicitly includes
both assessment timelines and the separately computed cutoff age. This is covered by a
regression test. The rerun correctly identifies the June Hajr assessment as one month old
at the July cutoff. Schema validity alone is not treated as factual correctness.

Cache replay is tested with an API stub that raises if any network request is attempted.
Requests, raw responses and validated outputs are cached. A persistent spend ledger keeps
conservative reservations for ambiguous failures, and a process lock prevents concurrent
runs from sharing the budget. Keep the cache to resume later. Output manifests distinguish
prior accounted spend from new-run estimates; these are estimates, not billing receipts.
The final six-example pilot has a conservative usage estimate of $0.125. Its cache replay
cost $0 in new API calls. The retained response/charge ledger accounts for about $0.447
across saved pilot requests; older pre-ledger failed attempts are not represented.

Later, run:

```sh
bash scripts/annotate_local.sh full
```

This requests all training examples, eight workers, with a conservative $185 accounting
ceiling. If the guard stops early or any request fails, completed annotations remain
cached and the manifest reports the incomplete result. Do not bypass the budget guard.
GPU rationale training requires complete, version-matched annotations and rejects a pilot
file. See the README for the completeness check and subsequent transfer commands.

## Reusable TimeNet connectors

Native PortWatch, ACLED, WFP and CHIRPS connectors implement the official TimeNet
BaseConnector contract, pinned to commit `c39ca32b64ad0c89ea54093dbcb285c1a93eb006`.
All four have verified TimeF write/read round trips using a Yemen January–March 2020
example. Calendar timestamps, null values, units and provenance survive the conversion.

The acquisition project is independently installable and can be extracted as a repository.
It is not yet published to an upstream registry. See
[connector documentation](../open-relief-data/README.md).

## Measured local baselines

Test-set results (2,230 examples; macro-F1 across classes present):

| Model | Macro-F1 | Accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|
| Training majority | 0.0752 | 0.1771 |
| Latest available IPC, majority fallback when absent | 0.7350 | 0.7744 |

Persistence issues no deterioration alerts on examples with a known baseline, so its
secondary deterioration recall is zero despite its strong phase accuracy.

Classical logistic-regression ablations use the **validation** partition (2,503 examples),
with preprocessing fitted on training only:

| Features | Macro-F1 | Accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|
| All sources | 0.5844 | 0.7000 |
| Food history and calendar only | 0.6032 | 0.7339 |
| Without shipping | 0.5927 | 0.7036 |
| Without conflict | 0.5113 | 0.6304 |
| Without rainfall | 0.5615 | 0.6772 |
| Without prices | 0.6104 | 0.7315 |

I've checked out the repo. Here's what I found and what I plan to do:

## 1. Hooks

- **`.claude/settings.json`** (actual Claude Code hooks) — already correct and confirmed working: `.entire/logs/entire.log` shows clean `session-start`/`turn-start` events for this session, no errors.
- **`.codex/hooks.json`** — this had Windows-only `cmd.exe` invocations (e.g. `cmd.exe /d /s /c "where.exe entire >nul..."`) that can't run on this Mac. It's already been patched in your working tree (uncommitted) to portable `sh -c 'command -v entire >/dev/null 2>&1 && exec entire hooks ... || exit 0'` forms. I validated the JSON — it's well-formed and consistent across all 6 hook events.

**Plan:** just commit this existing fix (no further changes needed to make hooks work).

## 2. Git commit

Stage and commit everything currently pending, **except** what's already (correctly) gitignored:
- Modified: `.codex/hooks.json` (hook fix), `README.md` (project rewrite)
- New: `.gitignore`, `.env.example`, `HANDOFF.md`, `configs/`, `docs/`, `open-relief-data/`, `pyproject.toml`, `refrences/`, `reports/`, `requirements-gpu.txt`, `requirements-local.lock.txt`, `scripts/`, `src/`, `task.md`, `tests/`
- Excluded (gitignored, correctly): `.venv/`, `.pytest_cache/`, `.env` (contains your real `OPENAI_API_KEY`/`HF_TOKEN` — confirmed not tracked), `.DS_Store`, `data/raw/`, `data/processed/`, `artifacts/`, `checkpoints/`

I'll double check `open-relief-data/` and `scripts/` for stray `__pycache__`/`.egg-info` before adding (already gitignore-covered, but will verify nothing sneaks in).

## 3. HuggingFace upload → `datasets/Alaeddinnn/OpenRelief`

- `huggingface_hub` isn't installed in the venv and no `hf`/`huggingface-cli` is on PATH — I'll `pip install -U huggingface_hub` into `.venv`. Your cached login token at `~/.cache/huggingface/token` is present, so no re-login needed.

153	    """Retain reservations for ambiguous API failures across process restarts."""
154	    charges = {p.name.removesuffix(".charge.json"): json.loads(p.read_text())["usd"]
155	               for p in cache.glob("*.charge.json")}
156	    for path in cache.glob("*.response.json"):
157	        key = path.name.removesuffix(".response.json")
158	        if key not in charges:
159	            charges[key] = usage_cost(json.loads(path.read_text()).get("usage") or {})
160	    return sum(charges.values())

163	def annotate(example: dict, model: str, cache: Path, client) -> dict:
164	    payload = request_payload(example, model)
165	    key = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
166	    cache.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
167	    path = cache / f"{key}.json"
168	    if path.exists():
169	        result = json.loads(path.read_text())
170	        validate_annotation(result["annotation"], example)
171	        result["sample_id"] = example["input"]["sample_id"]
172	        result["dataset_version"] = example["input"]["dataset_version"]
173	        return result
174	    raw_path = cache / f"{key}.response.json"
175	    unresolved_prior_charge = 0.0
176	    if raw_path.exists():
177	        from openai.types.chat import ChatCompletion
178	        response = ChatCompletion.model_validate(json.loads(raw_path.read_text()))
179	    else:
180	        charge_path = cache / f"{key}.charge.json"
181	        if charge_path.exists():
182	            unresolved_prior_charge = json.loads(charge_path.read_text())["usd"]
183	        charge_path.write_text(json.dumps({"usd": unresolved_prior_charge + maximum_cost(payload), "basis": "reserved_before_request"}))
184	        response = client.chat.completions.create(**payload)
185	    (cache / f"{key}.response.json").write_text(response.model_dump_json(indent=2) + "\n")
186	    if response.usage:
187	        if not unresolved_prior_charge and (cache / f"{key}.charge.json").exists() and raw_path.exists():
188	            # Retain any accumulated reservation from a previous ambiguous retry.
189	            previous = json.loads((cache / f"{key}.charge.json").read_text())
190	            if previous.get("basis") == "conservative_usage":
191	                unresolved_prior_charge = max(0, previous["usd"] - usage_cost(response.usage.model_dump()))
192	        (cache / f"{key}.charge.json").write_text(json.dumps({"usd": unresolved_prior_charge + usage_cost(response.usage.model_dump()), "basis": "conservative_usage"}))
193	    choice = response.choices[0]
194	    if choice.finish_reason != "stop" or choice.message.refusal or not choice.message.content:
195	        raise ValueError("Annotation refused, empty or truncated; no valid artifact cached")
196	    annotation = validate_annotation(json.loads(choice.message.content), example)
197	    result = {"sample_id": example["input"]["sample_id"], "dataset_version": example["input"]["dataset_version"],
198	        "purpose": "training_supervision_only", "request_sha256": key, "model": response.model,
199	        "request_id": response.id, "usage": response.usage.model_dump() if response.usage else {},
200	        "annotation": annotation.model_dump()}
201	    temporary = path.with_suffix(".tmp")
202	    temporary.write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
203	    temporary.replace(path)
204	    return result

207	def main():
208	    from dotenv import load_dotenv
209	    from openai import OpenAI
210	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
211	    parser.add_argument("dataset", type=Path)
212	    parser.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=3)
213	    parser.add_argument("--all", action="store_true", help="Annotate every training example, subject to budget")
214	    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=Path("artifacts/annotations-pilot.jsonl"))
215	    parser.add_argument("--cache", type=Path, default=Path("artifacts/annotation-cache"))
216	    parser.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=1)
217	    parser.add_argument("--budget-usd", type=float, default=190.0)
218	    args = parser.parse_args()
219	    if args.limit < 1:
220	        parser.error("--limit must be positive")
221	    if not 0 < args.budget_usd <= 190:
222	        parser.error("--budget-usd must be positive and at most 190 (reserve remains for pilots)")
223	    # One writer prevents concurrent runs from spending the same budget or cache entry.
224	    import fcntl
225	    args.cache.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
226	    run_lock = (args.cache / ".run.lock").open("a")
227	    try:
228	        fcntl.flock(run_lock, fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
229	    except BlockingIOError:
230	        parser.error("Another annotation run owns this cache; wait for it to finish")
231	    load_dotenv()
232	    base_url = os.getenv("OPENAI_BASE_URL", "https://api.openai.com/v1").rstrip("/")
233	    if base_url != "https://api.openai.com/v1":
234	        parser.error("This run is authorized for the official OpenAI API only")
235	    model = os.getenv("OPENAI_ANNOTATION_MODEL", "gpt-5.6-terra")
236	    if not os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"):
237	        parser.error("OPENAI_API_KEY is missing; configure .env")
238	    examples = load_examples(args.dataset, "train")
239	    # Deterministic diverse ordering instead of taking adjacent overlapping windows.
240	    examples.sort(key=lambda e: e["input"]["sample_id"])
241	    if not 1 <= args.workers <= 16:
242	        parser.error("--workers must be between 1 and 16")
243	    if model != "gpt-5.6-terra":
244	        parser.error("Cost guard is verified for gpt-5.6-terra; update pricing before changing model")
245	    selected = examples if args.all else select_pilot(examples, args.limit)
246	    # UTF-8 bytes bound ordinary text token count; include schema and protocol overhead.
247	    # No automatic retries: ambiguous network failures must not multiply reserved spend.
248	    bound = sum(((len(json.dumps(request_payload(e,model)).encode()) + 1000) * 2.5 + 4096 * 12) / 1_000_000 for e in selected)
249	    print(json.dumps({"requests":len(selected), "conservative_cost_bound_usd":round(bound,2)}),flush=True)
250	    client = OpenAI(base_url=base_url, timeout=120, max_retries=0)
251	    args.output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
252	    results, failures = [], []
253	    spent, reserved = prior_spend(args.cache), 0.0
254	    starting_spend = spent
255	    pending = iter(selected)
256	    deferred = None
257	    budget_exhausted = False
258	    with args.output.open("w") as handle, ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=args.workers) as pool:
259	        futures = {}
260	        exhausted = False
261	        while futures or not exhausted:
262	            while len(futures) < args.workers and not exhausted:
263	                example = deferred if deferred is not None else next(pending, None)
264	                deferred = None
265	                if example is None:
266	                    exhausted = True
267	                    break
268	                payload = request_payload(example, model)
269	                key = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
270	                cached = (args.cache / f"{key}.json").exists() or (args.cache / f"{key}.response.json").exists()
271	                ceiling = 0.0 if cached else maximum_cost(payload)
272	                if spent + reserved + ceiling > min(args.budget_usd,190):
273	                    deferred = example
274	                    if not futures:
275	                        budget_exhausted = True
276	                        exhausted = True
277	                    break
278	                futures[pool.submit(annotate,example,model,args.cache,client)] = (example,ceiling)
279	                reserved += ceiling
280	            if not futures:
281	                break
282	            done,_ = wait(futures,return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)
283	            for future in done:
284	                example,ceiling=futures.pop(future); reserved-=ceiling
285	                try:
286	                    result=future.result();results.append(result)
287	                    if ceiling:
288	                        spent+=usage_cost(result["usage"])
289	                    handle.write(json.dumps(result)+"\n");handle.flush()
290	                except Exception as error:
291	                    spent+=ceiling  # reserve worst case when usage is unavailable
292	                    failures.append({"sample_id":example["input"]["sample_id"],"error":str(error)})
293	                completed=len(results)+len(failures)
294	                if completed % 25 == 0 or completed == len(selected):
295	                    print(json.dumps({"completed":completed,"valid":len(results),"failures":len(failures),"accounted_cost_usd":round(spent,4)}),flush=True)
296	    results.sort(key=lambda r:r["sample_id"])
297	    args.output.write_text("".join(json.dumps(r)+"\n" for r in results))
298	    args.output.with_suffix(".manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps({"requested":len(selected),"valid":len(results),"budget_exhausted":budget_exhausted,"accounted_cost_usd":spent,
299	        "prior_cache_spend_usd": starting_spend, "new_run_accounted_cost_usd": spent - starting_spend,
300	        "failures":failures,"model":model,"conservative_cost_bound_usd":bound,
301	        "estimated_usage_usd":sum(usage_cost(r["usage"]) for r in results),
302	        "pricing_source":"https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.6-terra", "cached_usage_may_include_previous_runs":True},indent=2)+"\n")
303	    if budget_exhausted:
304	        raise SystemExit("Run budget reached; completed annotations retained")
305	    if failures:
306	        raise SystemExit(f"{len(failures)} annotations failed validation or API access; see manifest and rerun to reuse cache")
307

309	if __name__ == "__main__":
310	    main()

1	You are an expert AI/ML engineer, time-series researcher, and systems architect. We are building a hackathon prototype called **Open Relief**.
2	
3	Your job is to understand the project, inspect the available documentation and repository, resolve important ambiguities, create a concrete implementation plan, and then execute that plan step by step.
4	
5	# 1. Project Goal
6	
7	**Open Relief** is an early-warning system for predicting future deterioration in food security across countries and regions.
8	
9	The core hypothesis is that changes in food insecurity can be predicted ahead of time by combining heterogeneous temporal signals such as:
10	
11	* maritime trade and shipping activity;
12	* imports and exports;
13	* port activity;
14	* weather and rainfall;
15	* conflict and security incidents;
16	* other socioeconomic, logistics, climate, and crisis-related signals defined in `HANDOFF.md`.
17	
18	`HANDOFF.md` is the authoritative project-level source for the datasets, target variables, terminology, geographic coverage, temporal resolutions, and known data sources.
19	
20	**Read `HANDOFF.md` completely before proposing the final architecture. Do not invent replacements for datasets that the handbook already specifies unless there is a technical reason to do so.**
21	
22	One important source is **IMF PortWatch**, which provides high-frequency maritime activity data derived from vessel movements and port activity. Use the official PortWatch platform/API and determine which specific datasets and endpoints are appropriate for this project.
23	
24	The eventual product should be explainable as:
25	
26	> **Open Relief is a multimodal time-series early-warning model that integrates trade, shipping, weather, conflict, and other signals to predict worsening food insecurity before it becomes visible in conventional lagging indicators.**
27	
28	This is a hackathon prototype, so prioritize a technically credible, demonstrable, reproducible end-to-end system over unnecessary production complexity.
29	
30	# 2. First Task: Understand the Existing Context
31	
32	Before writing significant implementation code:
33	
34	1. Read `HANDOFF.md` in full.
35	2. Inspect the existing repository, documentation, configuration, scripts, and datasets.
36	3. Identify every data source described in the handbook.
37	4. Identify the food-security target or index we are ultimately trying to predict.
38	5. Determine the available time range, temporal resolution, geographic resolution, and update frequency for each source.
39	6. Determine which parts of the system already exist and which must be built.
40	7. Inspect the official **OpenTSLM** implementation and documentation.
41	8. Verify any external framework, dataset, API, or library whose identity or usage is uncertain rather than guessing.
42	
43	When something important is genuinely ambiguous, ask me targeted clarifying questions.
44	
45	Group the important questions together rather than interrupting implementation repeatedly.
46	
47	In particular, clarify anything that materially affects:
48	
49	* the definition of the prediction target;
50	* forecast horizon;
51	* geographic unit;
52	* time resolution;
53	* train/validation/test periods;
54	* repository boundaries;
55	* OpenTSLM fine-tuning approach;
56	* data licensing or accessibility;
57	* compute constraints;
58	* hackathon demo requirements.
59	
60	Do not ask questions whose answers can reasonably be obtained by reading the repository, `HANDOFF.md`, or authoritative documentation.
61	
62	# 3. Proposed System Architecture
63	
64	The project should be organized around several major components.
65	
66	## A. Data Acquisition Repository
67	
68	Create or design a **separate data-acquisition repository** responsible for retrieving and preparing the external datasets used by Open Relief.
69	
70	This repository should contain:
71	
72	* download scripts;
73	* API clients;
74	* scheduled-fetch scripts where appropriate;
75	* source-specific connectors;
76	* caching;
77	* validation;
78	* retries and error handling;
79	* raw-data versioning conventions;
80	* metadata describing provenance;
81	* timestamps indicating when data became available;
82	* standardized intermediate outputs.
83	
84	Examples include the sources defined in `HANDOFF.md`, particularly maritime/trade signals from IMF PortWatch, rainfall/weather information, conflict or incident data, and any other relevant inputs.
85	
86	The PortWatch integration should evaluate the appropriate official interfaces for retrieving the daily port activity, shipment, trade, import/export, or related maritime indicators required by the project.
87	
88	Where possible, preserve both:
89	
90	* `event_time`: when an observation actually occurred;
91	* `availability_time`: when that observation would realistically have become available to a forecaster.
92	
93	This distinction will help prevent accidental look-ahead bias.
94	
95	## B. Standardized Data Connector
96	
97	The acquisition repository must expose a clean connector or adapter that converts the collected data into the standardized multivariate time-series representation expected by the Open Relief modeling pipeline.
98	
99	Because this is a hackathon handoff, another team should be able to clone the repositories and understand:
100	
101	* where the data comes from;
102	* how to fetch it;
103	* how it is transformed;
104	* how it becomes model input;
105	* which version of the data was used for experiments.
106	
107	The handoff should not depend on undocumented local files.
108	
109	# 4. Dataset Construction
110	
111	Create a reproducible dataset-building pipeline that aligns heterogeneous data sources across:
112	
113	* time;
114	* country/region;
115	* frequency;
116	* missing values;
117	* feature definitions.
118	
119	Determine an appropriate canonical time frequency after inspecting the available sources.
120	
121	Do not assume everything needs to be daily if another temporal resolution produces a more meaningful and reliable modeling task.
122	
123	The pipeline should distinguish:
124	
125	* raw observations;
126	* transformed features;
127	* prediction targets;
128	* metadata;
129	* training splits;
130	* optional LLM annotations.
131	
132	Document all important:
133	
134	* resampling;
135	* aggregation;
136	* interpolation;
137	* normalization;
138	* missing-data handling;
139	* feature transformations.
140	
141	Never silently fill a historical input with information that would only have been known in the future.
142	
143	# 5. Prediction Target
144	
145	Determine the exact food-security outcome from `HANDOFF.md`.
146	
147	Do not prematurely assume whether this is:
148	
149	* binary classification;
150	* multiclass classification;
151	* ordinal classification;
152	* regression;
153	* change-point prediction;
154	* threshold-crossing prediction;
155	* natural-language prediction plus structured label;
156	* or some combination of these.
157	
158	The primary task should represent something operationally meaningful, for example predicting whether food insecurity will significantly worsen within a future forecast horizon.
159	
160	If the target definition is not sufficiently specified in the handbook, ask me before locking the modeling design.
161	
162	The final target formulation should clearly specify:
163	
164	* observation date;
165	* prediction cutoff;
166	* forecast horizon;
167	* geographic unit;
168	* definition of a worsening event;
169	* expected model output.
170	
171	Because OpenTSLM is capable of generating language as well as reasoning over time-series signals, also evaluate whether the model should jointly produce:
172	
173	1. a structured prediction; and
174	2. a concise natural-language rationale.
175	
176	However, the quantitative prediction must remain measurable independently of the explanation.
177	
178	# 6. LLM-Assisted Annotation Pipeline
179	
180	Build a separate annotation component that communicates with an **OpenAI-compatible endpoint**.
181	
182	For the prototype, use the official OpenAI API.
183	
184	The objective is to enrich historical training examples with interpretations of how observed time-series patterns may relate to later changes in food security.
185	
186	For a historical example, the annotation model may receive:
187	
188	* historical multivariate time-series information;
189	* descriptions of the signals;
190	* the subsequent observed food-security outcome;
191	* relevant metadata;
192	* optionally retrieved historical context.
193	
194	The annotation model should produce structured outputs describing things such as:
195	
196	* whether a meaningful deterioration occurred;
197	* important precursor patterns;
198	* which variables changed;
199	* the temporal ordering of those changes;
200	* unusual or anomalous signals;
201	* plausible relationships between signals;
202	* relevant historical events;
203	* a concise explanation of the episode;
204	* confidence or uncertainty.
205	
206	Use a strict JSON schema or another validated machine-readable output format whenever practical.
207	
208	# 7. Using LLM Historical Knowledge
209	
210	The annotation LLM **may use its internal historical knowledge** when that knowledge is useful.
211	
212	For example, the model may already know that during a particular period a country experienced:
213	
214	* a war;
215	* political instability;
216	* port disruption;
217	* drought;
218	* flooding;
219	* sanctions;
220	* a major economic shock;
221	* an agricultural crisis;
222	* a supply-chain disruption.
223	
224	Do not artificially prevent the model from using this knowledge.
225	
226	If the model is confident that a well-known historical event is relevant, it may include it as contextual information.
227	
228	However, maintain reasonable provenance.
229	
230	Where practical, distinguish between:
231	
232	* **observed evidence** — directly present in our datasets;
233	* **retrieved evidence** — obtained from an external source;
234	* **model-recalled context** — supplied from the LLM's internal knowledge;
235	* **inference** — a relationship the model believes is plausible.
236	
237	The purpose is not to prohibit model knowledge. The purpose is to avoid silently confusing an uncertain recollection with an observed fact.
238	
239	For hackathon purposes, do not require external verification of every historical statement.
240	
241	A sensible policy is:
242	
243	* allow confident model knowledge;
244	* retrieve external evidence for important or uncertain claims when feasible;
245	* record uncertainty when the model is unsure;
246	* avoid treating speculative causal explanations as certain facts.
247	
248	The annotation prompt should explicitly encourage the model to say when it is uncertain rather than hallucinating an explanation.
249	
250	# 8. Prediction Labels vs. Explanatory Annotations
251	
252	Keep the distinction between the objective target and the LLM-generated explanation clear.
253	
254	For example:
255	
256	### Ground-truth target
257	
258	Derived from the actual future food-security index or other objective target defined in `HANDOFF.md`.
259	
260	### Annotation
261	
262	An LLM-generated interpretation describing what patterns or historical circumstances may have contributed to that target transition.
263	
264	The LLM should therefore not arbitrarily decide the ground-truth outcome when an objective label can be computed from the actual food-security dataset.
265	
266	Instead, the LLM enriches that label with temporal reasoning and context.
267	
268	If there are cases where the food-security target itself requires interpretation, document exactly how the annotation model contributes to label generation.
269	
270	# 9. Temporal Leakage and LLM Annotations
271	
272	Temporal leakage must be handled carefully, but do not make the implementation unnecessarily restrictive.
273	
274	For each training example, explicitly identify:
275	
276	`INPUT WINDOW → PREDICTION CUTOFF → FUTURE TARGET WINDOW`
277	
278	The forecasting input must only contain information that would have been available at the prediction cutoff.
279	
280	However, during **training-data annotation**, the annotation model may inspect the future outcome because its role is to explain why that historical training example received its label.
281	
282	For example:
283	
284	`historical signals + known future deterioration → explanatory training annotation`
285	
286	This can be legitimate supervision.
287	
288	The critical question is whether information from the future subsequently leaks into something that the deployed model receives before making its prediction.
289	
290	Therefore distinguish:
291	
292	* input features;
293	* prediction labels;
294	* LLM-generated supervision;
295	* explanatory annotations;
296	* evaluation metadata.
297	
298	Audit this explicitly.
299	
300	If we intentionally experiment with LLM-generated rationales as training supervision, design the training process so that the model does not require unavailable future information during inference.
301	
302	# 10. Core Model: OpenTSLM
303	
304	The primary model for this project is **OpenTSLM — Open Time-Series Language Models**.
305	
306	Do **not** substitute OpenLTM, Timer, Timer-XL, or a conventional LSTM unless they are being used strictly as comparison baselines.
307	
308	OpenTSLM treats time series as a native modality alongside language, allowing a language model to reason directly over temporal signals.
309	
310	This is especially relevant to Open Relief because our system needs to combine multiple time-series signals and ideally produce both:
311	
312	* predictions;
313	* interpretable reasoning/explanations.
314	
315	Inspect the current official OpenTSLM repository, paper, pretrained checkpoints, and documentation before implementing the model pipeline.
316	
317	The official project currently includes architectures such as:
318	
319	* **OpenTSLM-SP** — soft-prompt-based time-series integration;
320	* **OpenTSLM-Flamingo** — cross-attention-based integration inspired by Flamingo.
321	
322	Do not assume beforehand which architecture is best for Open Relief.
323	
324	Investigate both and determine which is most practical for our dataset, compute budget, and hackathon timeline.
325	
326	OpenTSLM currently supports pretrained language-model backbones such as Llama and Gemma variants and provides pretrained model loading and fine-tuning infrastructure.
327	
328	Use the existing OpenTSLM implementation rather than reimplementing the architecture from scratch unless absolutely necessary.
329	
330	# 11. Adapting OpenTSLM to Open Relief
331	
332	OpenTSLM was originally demonstrated heavily on medical and general time-series reasoning tasks.
333	
334	Our task is to adapt the architecture to a new domain:
335	
336	**multivariate geopolitical, climate, trade, logistics, and food-security time series.**
337	
338	Determine how our data should be represented using OpenTSLM's expected input format.
339	
340	Investigate:
341	
342	* how individual time series are encoded;
343	* how multiple time series are interleaved;
344	* how textual descriptions of each signal are supplied;
345	* expected patch sizes;
346	* variable sequence lengths;
347	* normalization requirements;
348	* context-window constraints;
349	* how the model handles multiple time-series channels;
350	* how prompts and time-series chunks should be structured.
351	
352	A conceptual Open Relief sample may contain:
353	
354	* shipping-volume series;
355	* import-volume series;
356	* rainfall series;
357	* conflict-event series;
358	* commodity or food-price series;
359	* food-security history;
360	* textual metadata describing the country and each signal.
361	
362	The model might then receive a question such as:
363	
364	> Based only on the information available up to this date, is food insecurity in this region likely to deteriorate within the next N weeks/months? Explain the temporal signals that support your prediction.
365	
366	The exact prompt and output schema should be determined experimentally.
367	
368	# 12. OpenTSLM Training Dataset
369	
370	Create an OpenTSLM-compatible training dataset from the unified Open Relief dataset.
371	
372	Each sample should include the appropriate combination of:
373	
374	* time-series tensors;
375	* descriptions of those series;
376	* geographic context;
377	* prediction cutoff;
378	* question/instruction;
379	* structured prediction target;
380	* optional explanatory target.
381	
382	If helpful, use the annotation pipeline to produce richer supervised examples resembling:
383	
384	**Input**
385	
386	Historical time series from multiple sources.
387	
388	**Question**
389	
390	What is likely to happen to food security over the defined forecast horizon?
391	
392	**Target answer**
393	
394	A structured outcome plus reasoning.
395	
396	For example conceptually:
397	
398	`Risk: HIGH`
399	
400	`Expected direction: DETERIORATING`
401	
402	`Confidence: 0.82`
403	
404	`Reasoning: Maritime imports have declined for several weeks while conflict incidents and rainfall anomalies have increased...`
405	
406	Do not hard-code this exact format unless it proves suitable for OpenTSLM training.
407	
408	# 13. Baseline OpenTSLM Evaluation
409	
410	Before fine-tuning, establish a baseline using the original/pretrained OpenTSLM model.
411	
412	The baseline should answer:
413	
414	> How capable is OpenTSLM at this task before being adapted to Open Relief?
415	
416	Use the closest appropriate pretrained OpenTSLM checkpoint and a reproducible evaluation prompt.
417	
418	Evaluate it on a held-out subset before Open Relief fine-tuning.
419	
420	If direct zero-shot evaluation is meaningful, include it.
421	
422	If minimal task adaptation is required for the model to produce a valid output, document that clearly.
423	
424	Also consider one simple non-OpenTSLM baseline if it can be implemented cheaply.
425	
426	The core comparison remains:
427	
428	**pretrained OpenTSLM → Open Relief fine-tuned OpenTSLM**
429	
430	# 14. Fine-Tuning OpenTSLM
431	
432	Fine-tune OpenTSLM on the Open Relief dataset.
433	
434	Use the official OpenTSLM training infrastructure as much as possible.
435	
436	Determine whether **OpenTSLM-SP** or **OpenTSLM-Flamingo** is preferable based on:
437	
438	* GPU/VRAM requirements;
439	* training speed;
440	* multimodal capacity;
441	* number of time series per example;
442	* quality of temporal reasoning;
443	* implementation maturity;
444	* fine-tuning complexity;
445	* hackathon constraints.
446	
447	If compute allows, a small preliminary comparison between the two architectures is useful.
448	
449	Otherwise, select one, document the reasoning, and proceed.
450	
451	The training pipeline should track:
452	
453	* base OpenTSLM checkpoint;
454	* LLM backbone;
455	* OpenTSLM architecture;
456	* dataset version;
457	* feature configuration;
458	* forecast horizon;
459	* training range;
460	* validation range;
461	* test range;
462	* hyperparameters;
463	* random seed;
464	* experiment metrics.
465	
466	The primary experiment is:
467	
468	**Pretrained OpenTSLM → Open Relief fine-tuning → held-out evaluation**
469	
470	# 15. Evaluation and Leakage Prevention
471	
472	Evaluation quality is one of the most important parts of the project.
473	
474	Do not randomly shuffle temporally related observations into train and test sets if doing so would expose future information.
475	
476	Prefer chronological evaluation.
477	
478	Conceptually:
479	
480	`TRAIN → VALIDATION → TEST`
481	
482	where the test period represents genuinely later observations.
483	
484	Consider rolling-origin or walk-forward evaluation if feasible.
485	
486	Also consider geographic generalization if the data permit it:
487	
488	* future periods in countries represented during training;
489	* unseen countries or regions;
490	* crisis episodes not represented during training.
491	
492	The exact quantitative metrics depend on the final target.
493	
494	For deterioration-event prediction, useful metrics may include:
495	
496	* precision;
497	* recall;
498	* F1;
499	* PR-AUC;
500	* ROC-AUC;
501	* calibration;
502	* lead time before deterioration.
503	
504	For regression or ordinal forecasting, select appropriate alternatives.
505	
506	Because this is an early-warning system, **lead time** is particularly important.
507	
508	A model that correctly identifies a crisis several weeks earlier may be substantially more useful than one that only becomes confident when the deterioration is already obvious.
509	
510	# 16. Evaluate Explanations Separately
511	
512	OpenTSLM may produce natural-language reasoning in addition to the quantitative prediction.
513	
514	Evaluate these two capabilities separately.
515	
516	### Prediction quality
517	
518	Does the model correctly predict future deterioration?
519	
520	### Explanation quality
521	
522	Does the explanation correctly identify relevant patterns in the input data?
523	
524	Do not allow an impressive-sounding explanation to compensate for an incorrect prediction.
525	
526	For selected examples, compare the model's reasoning against:
527	
528	* actual time-series changes;
529	* LLM annotations;
530	* known historical events;
531	* retrieved evidence where available.
532	
533	# 17. Core Hackathon Demonstration
534	
535	The final experiment should make the following comparison extremely clear.
536	
537	### Baseline
538	
539	Original/pretrained OpenTSLM before Open Relief fine-tuning.
540	
541	### Open Relief
542	
543	The same OpenTSLM architecture after domain-specific fine-tuning on our multimodal crisis dataset.
544	
545	### Result
546	
547	Measure whether fine-tuning improves the model's ability to predict food-security deterioration on unseen future periods.
548	
549	Show a concise benchmark table.
550	
551	For example:
552	
553	| Model         |  F1 | Recall | PR-AUC | Mean Warning Lead Time |
554	| ------------- | --: | -----: | -----: | ---------------------: |
555	| Base OpenTSLM | ... |    ... |    ... |                    ... |
556	| Open Relief   | ... |    ... |    ... |                    ... |
557	
558	Use the actual metrics appropriate to the final task rather than blindly using these examples.
559	
560	Also create one or two strong visual case studies.
561	
562	For example:
563	
564	`shipping decline`
565	↓
566	`rainfall anomaly`
567	↓
568	`conflict escalation`
569	↓
570	`import decline`
571	↓
572	`Open Relief warning`
573	↓
574	`observed food-security deterioration`
575	
576	Show the model prediction **before** the observed deterioration whenever possible.
577	
578	# 18. Explainability
579	
580	A major advantage of using OpenTSLM should be its ability to reason over time-series signals rather than simply outputting a number.
581	
582	For selected predictions, produce human-readable explanations showing which signals the model considered relevant.
583	
584	For example:
585	
586	> Maritime import volumes began declining six weeks before the prediction cutoff. During the same period, conflict incidents rose sharply and rainfall remained below the historical seasonal range. Together, these patterns are consistent with increased food-security risk over the next forecast window.
587	
588	These explanations may combine:
589	
590	* direct observations;
591	* learned temporal patterns;
592	* LLM historical knowledge;
593	* retrieved context.
594	
595	Where appropriate, differentiate between what the data directly shows and what the model is inferring.
596	
597	Do not require every explanation to be externally cited, but verify particularly important, surprising, or uncertain historical claims when practical.
598	
599	# 19. Repository Structure
600	
601	Design the project so another engineer can understand and reproduce it after the hackathon.
602	
603	A reasonable high-level separation might be:
604	
605	`open-relief-data/`
606	
607	* acquisition;
608	* source connectors;
609	* normalization;
610	* standardized outputs.
611	
612	`open-relief/`
613	
614	* dataset construction;
615	* annotation;
616	* OpenTSLM adapters;
617	* training;
618	* evaluation;
619	* visualization;
620	* demo.
621	
622	Do not force this exact structure if the existing repositories suggest something better.
623	
624	Prefer:
625	
626	* Python;

629	* configuration files rather than hard-coded parameters;
630	* deterministic dataset creation;
631	* environment-variable API keys;
632	* clear READMEs;
633	* explicit CLI commands;
634	* tests for important transformations;
635	* tests for temporal leakage.
636	
637	Never commit secrets or API keys.
638	
639	Include `.env.example` where appropriate.
640	
641	# 20. Reproducibility
642	
643	Another team member should be able to reproduce the central experiment.
644	
645	Document commands similar in spirit to:
646	
647	`fetch data`
648	
649	`build dataset`
650

660	
661	The actual CLI design is up to you.
662	
663	Cache expensive intermediate results where appropriate, especially:
664	
665	* downloaded external data;
666	* processed datasets;
667	* OpenAI annotation responses;
668	* trained model checkpoints.
669	
670	# 21. Expected Deliverables

672	By the end of the implementation, aim to have:
673	
674	1. a reproducible data-acquisition repository;
675	2. standardized source connectors;
676	3. a unified multivariate time-series dataset;

679	6. an OpenTSLM-compatible dataset adapter;

684	11. example model explanations;
685	12. prediction visualizations;
686	13. documentation describing architecture and reproduction steps;
687	14. a concise hackathon demo path.
688	
689	# 22. How You Should Work

691	Follow this process.

693	## Phase 1 — Discovery

695	Inspect:

"""Run the identical held-out cohort before/after adapting official OpenTSLM.

The small explicit loop reuses official architecture, compute_loss, collator,
LoRA and checkpoint methods. Batch size one avoids upstream SP's unmasked padded
answer tokens; gradient accumulation controls effective batch size.
"""
import argparse
import copy
import hashlib
import json
import math
from pathlib import Path
import random
from .adapter import format_input, format_training
from .dataset import load_examples, digest_file
from .evaluate import parse_prediction, score

UPSTREAM_COMMIT = "2968f4b891baab4307f7e9d0043e87677b593a30"


def main():
    p=argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("dataset",type=Path)
    p.add_argument("--annotations",type=Path)
    p.add_argument("--output",type=Path,default=Path("artifacts/gpu-run"))
    p.add_argument("--checkpoint",default="OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-sp")
    p.add_argument("--revision",default="main")
    p.add_argument("--epochs",type=int,default=10)
    p.add_argument("--patience",type=int,default=3)
    p.add_argument("--accumulate",type=int,default=8)
    p.add_argument("--eval-limit",type=int,default=256)
    p.add_argument("--drop-source",action="append",default=[])
    p.add_argument("--seed",type=int,default=42)
    a=p.parse_args()
    if min(a.epochs,a.accumulate,a.eval_limit,a.patience)<1:
        p.error("Epochs, accumulation, evaluation limit and patience must be positive")
    import torch
    import numpy as np
    from huggingface_hub import HfApi, hf_hub_download, snapshot_download
    from opentslm.model.llm.OpenTSLMSP import OpenTSLMSP
    from opentslm.model.llm.OpenTSLMFlamingo import OpenTSLMFlamingo
    from opentslm.time_series_datasets.util import extend_time_series_to_match_patch_size_and_aggregate
    if not torch.cuda.is_available():
        p.error("Run on the GPU training machine with CUDA available")
    random.seed(a.seed); np.random.seed(a.seed); torch.manual_seed(a.seed); torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(a.seed)
    if a.output.exists() and any(a.output.iterdir()):
        p.error("Choose an empty output directory to preserve previous experiments")
    a.output.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
    train=load_examples(a.dataset,"train")
    val=sorted(load_examples(a.dataset,"validation"),key=lambda e:e["input"]["sample_id"])[:a.eval_limit]
    test=sorted(load_examples(a.dataset,"test"),key=lambda e:e["input"]["sample_id"])[:a.eval_limit]
    annotations={}
    if a.annotations:
        annotations={r["sample_id"]:r for r in map(json.loads,a.annotations.read_text().splitlines())}
        ids = {e["input"]["sample_id"] for e in train}
        if set(annotations) != ids:
            p.error("Annotations must cover the full training partition. Finish annotation first, or omit --annotations for phase-only training.")
        for e in train:
            format_training(e, "", annotations[e["input"]["sample_id"]])
    api=HfApi(); checkpoint_sha=api.model_info(a.checkpoint,revision=a.revision).sha
    if not a.checkpoint.startswith("OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-"):
        p.error("This reproducible runner currently supports official Llama 3.2 1B SP/Flamingo checkpoints")
    backbone="meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B"
    backbone_sha=api.model_info(backbone).sha
    backbone_path=snapshot_download(backbone,revision=backbone_sha)
    path=hf_hub_download(a.checkpoint,"model_checkpoint.pt",revision=checkpoint_sha)
    if a.checkpoint.endswith("-sp"):
        model=OpenTSLMSP(llm_id=backbone_path,device="cuda")
    elif a.checkpoint.endswith("-flamingo"):
        model=OpenTSLMFlamingo(llm_id=backbone_path,device="cuda",cross_attn_every_n_layers=1,gradient_checkpointing=False)
    else:

    model.load_from_file(path)
    eos=model.get_eos_token()
    patch_size=getattr(model,"patch_size",4)
    def collate(sample):
        return extend_time_series_to_match_patch_size_and_aggregate([sample],patch_size=patch_size,normalize=False)
    manifest={"upstream_commit":UPSTREAM_COMMIT,"checkpoint":a.checkpoint,"checkpoint_revision":checkpoint_sha,
        "backbone":backbone,"backbone_revision":backbone_sha,"checkpoint_sha256":digest_file(Path(path)),
        "dataset":json.loads((a.dataset/"manifest.json").read_text()),"seed":a.seed,
        "epochs":a.epochs,"patience":a.patience,"effective_batch_size":a.accumulate,"patch_size":patch_size,
        "drop_sources":a.drop_source,"annotation_sha256":digest_file(a.annotations) if a.annotations else None,
        "test_ids":[e["input"]["sample_id"] for e in test],"validation_ids":[e["input"]["sample_id"] for e in val],
        "validation_criterion":"Phase-only JSON prefix loss; rationale generation evaluated separately",
        "torch":torch.__version__,"gpu":torch.cuda.get_device_name(),"normalization":"input-window minmax, masks"}
    (a.output/"run.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest,indent=2)+"\n")
    def evaluate(name):

    before=evaluate("pretrained")

    groups=[]

            groups.append({"params":[parameter],"lr":1e-4 if "projector" in name else 2e-4,"weight_decay":0.01})
    optimizer=torch.optim.AdamW(groups)
    steps_per_epoch=math.ceil(len(train)/a.accumulate)
    total_steps=steps_per_epoch*a.epochs; warmup=max(1,int(total_steps*0.1))
    scheduler=torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(optimizer,lambda step: min((step+1)/warmup,max(0,(total_steps-step)/max(1,total_steps-warmup))))
    best=float("inf"); stale=0; log=[]
    for epoch in range(a.epochs):
        random.Random(a.seed+epoch).shuffle(train); model.train(); optimizer.zero_grad(); losses=[]
        for i,e in enumerate(train):
            sample=format_training(e,eos,annotations.get(e["input"]["sample_id"]),tuple(a.drop_source))
            loss=model.compute_loss(collate(sample))
            if not torch.isfinite(loss):raise RuntimeError("Non-finite training loss")
            group_size=min(a.accumulate,len(train)-(i//a.accumulate)*a.accumulate)
            (loss/group_size).backward(); losses.append(loss.item())
            if (i+1)%a.accumulate==0 or i+1==len(train):
                torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_([p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad],1.0)
                optimizer.step(); scheduler.step(); optimizer.zero_grad()
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            validation_losses = []
            for e in val:
                item = format_input(e["input"], tuple(a.drop_source))
                item["answer"] = '{"phase": ' + str(e["target"]["phase"]) + ','
                validation_losses.append(model.compute_loss(collate(item)).item())
            validation = sum(validation_losses) / len(validation_losses)
        log.append({"epoch":epoch+1,"train_loss":sum(losses)/len(losses),"validation_loss":validation})
        (a.output/"losses.json").write_text(json.dumps(log,indent=2)+"\n")
        print(json.dumps(log[-1]),flush=True)
        if validation<best:
            best=validation; stale=0; model.store_to_file(str(a.output/"best_model.pt"))
        else:stale+=1
        if stale>=a.patience:break
    model.load_from_file(str(a.output/"best_model.pt"))
    after=evaluate("fine_tuned")
    lines=["| Model | Macro-F1 (present classes) | Accuracy | Invalid output |", "|---|---:|---:|---:|"]
    for name,m in (("Pretrained OpenTSLM",before),("Open Relief fine-tuned",after)):
        lines.append(f"| {name} | {m['macro_f1_present_classes']:.4f} | {m['accuracy']:.4f} | {m['invalid_rate']:.4f} |")
    (a.output/"benchmark.md").write_text("\n".join(lines)+"\n")


if __name__=="__main__":main()

Read `HANDOFF.md` for the original measurements. Unknown publication lags stay unknown.
“Open” describes tested access, not unrestricted redistribution rights.

| Source | Event range / cadence | Geography | Access and implementation role |

| ACLED direct | Coverage/account dependent | Event-level | Gated OAuth service; do not use old unresolved hostname |
| UCDP GED | Version-dependent; lag unknown | Geocoded events | Handoff API returned 401 requiring token; optional comparison, no access bypass |

| WorldPop | Queried series 2000–2020, annual; newer products distinct | Population raster | Official API and raster URLs; optional lagged population weights, not a label |
| FEWS seasonal calendars/current coverage | Country-specific calendars, current regional coverage 2026 | Country/region | Qualitative rainfall/harvest context; current coverage is not historical coverage |
| OpenTSLM paper/checkpoints | Research artifacts, not forecasting observations | N/A | Official project, paper and HF model cards inspected |

## Official URLs

- PortWatch catalog: https://portwatch.imf.org/api/feed/dcat-us/1.1.json
- Ports item metadata: https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/83b1bbc7b3354c5fb1f40673bb8f852e?f=pjson
- Resolved layer: https://services9.arcgis.com/weJ1QsnbMYJlCHdG/arcgis/rest/services/Daily_Ports_Data/FeatureServer/0
- Bulk CSV: https://portwatch.imf.org/api/download/v1/items/83b1bbc7b3354c5fb1f40673bb8f852e/csv?layers=0
- PortWatch methods: https://portwatch.imf.org/pages/data-and-methodology
- PortWatch item links its license to https://www.imf.org/external/terms.htm
- CHIRPS: https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS-2.0/global_monthly/tifs/
- ACLED HDX metadata: https://data.humdata.org/api/3/action/package_show?id=yemen-acled-conflict-data
- WFP HDX metadata: https://data.humdata.org/api/3/action/package_show?id=wfp-food-prices-for-yemen
- WorldPop: https://hub.worldpop.org/rest/data/pop/wpgp?iso3=YEM
- UCDP: https://ucdpapi.pcr.uu.se/api/gedevents/25.1
- FEWS: https://fews.net
- OpenTSLM code: https://github.com/OpenTSLM/OpenTSLM
- Website: https://www.opentslm.com
- Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02410 (local v3 PDF inspected)
- SP: https://huggingface.co/OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-sp
- Flamingo: https://huggingface.co/OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-flamingo
- Annotation API: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs

The live PortWatch layer has maximum 1,000 records/query, pagination and order-by support,
and `date` is DateOnly. The connector filters verified integer year/month/day fields.
Raw port imports represent all dry bulk, not food imports specifically.

## OpenTSLM findings

Pinned source commit: `2968f4b891baab4307f7e9d0043e87677b593a30`.
Official sample dictionaries contain parallel lists of 1-D numeric series and descriptions.
Collation pads to a multiple of patch size (current default 4) and mutates the input sample.
Six monthly points are padded to eight positions, requiring two patches/channel;
checkpoint encoder configuration must be inspected rather than trusting a global default.
The paper describes [-1,1] inputs with original scale in text; current collation optionally
z-scores instead. Choose/document one input-only transform explicitly and use it identically
before and after fine-tuning. Do not upsample months into synthetic daily detail.

SP concatenates projected series tokens with language; Flamingo uses a separate series
modality with cross-attention and a resampler. SP is a reasonable short-input candidate,
not a measured winner. Both official TSQA 1B checkpoint pages exist; the Flamingo card's
example mistakenly uses the SP repository ID and legacy imports, so use current source.
Backbones can require Hugging Face access; run official checkpoints on CUDA (or CPU),
not MPS. No local training or full checkpoint download is planned.

## Final implementation notes

The configured acquisition covers 16 countries. ACLED source tables vary between national
and district aggregates; the modeling inputs use national monthly totals. WFP selects the
best-covered training-period staple commodity and exact package unit, excluding services
such as wheat milling costs. CHIRPS v2 rasters are aggregated to countries using fixed
geoBoundaries gbOpen ADM0 polygons; actual values and provenance are cached locally.
HFID and national signals assume one-month release lags, except CHIRPS at two months.
These assumptions do not recover missing historical release or revision records.

Actual TimeNet source: https://github.com/OpenTSLM/TimeNet/tree/c39ca32b64ad0c89ea54093dbcb285c1a93eb006
Documentation: https://docs.timenet.ai/
Native connectors implement BaseConnector download/convert and produce TimeFDataset,
with TimeFWriter/TimeFReader round-trip verification. They are not published upstream.

Annotation uses gpt-5.6-terra, selected for cost and quality after rejecting GPT-4o for the
final workflow. Model reference: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.6-terra
The cost guard charges conservatively at $2.50/M input tokens and $12/M output tokens,
without cache-read discounts, and reserves a byte-based input ceiling plus maximum output
for requests whose usage is unknown. Check current pricing before changing the model.

"""Causal monthly features computed from existing input observations only."""
import copy


def add_derived_channels(sample):
    channels = {c["name"]: c for c in sample["channels"]}
    specs = [
        ("wfp_staple_price", "change_1m_pct", 1, "percent_change", "%"),
        ("wfp_staple_price", "change_3m_pct", 3, "percent_change", "%"),
        ("acled_events", "sum_3m", 3, "sum", "events"),
        ("portwatch_import_cargo", "vs_previous_3m_pct", 3, "relative_mean", "%"),
    ]
    for source in ("fcs_rt mean", "rcsi_rt mean"):
        specs.extend((source, f"change_{lag}m", lag, "difference", "normalized index difference")
                     for lag in (1, 3))
    for source, suffix, lag, operation, unit in specs:
        if source not in channels:
            continue
        original = channels[source]
        values, times = [], []
        for i in range(len(original["values"])):
            if operation == "sum":
                indices = list(range(i - lag + 1, i + 1))
            elif operation == "relative_mean":
                indices = list(range(i - lag, i + 1))
            else:
                indices = [i - lag, i]
            value = available = None
            if min(indices) >= 0 and all(original["values"][j] is not None for j in indices):
                observations = [original["values"][j] for j in indices]
                if operation == "sum":
                    value = sum(observations)
                elif operation == "difference":
                    value = observations[-1] - observations[0]
                else:
                    denominator = (sum(observations[:-1]) / lag if operation == "relative_mean"
                                   else observations[0])
                    if denominator > 0:
                        value = 100 * (observations[-1] / denominator - 1)
                if value is not None:
                    available = max(original["availability_times"][j] for j in indices)
            values.append(value)
            times.append(available)
        channel = copy.deepcopy(original)
        channel.update(name=f"{source}_{suffix}", values=values, availability_times=times, unit=unit,
                       derived_from=[source],
                       description=f"{operation}, lag/window {lag} months; trailing input observations only. "
                                   "Insufficient history, missing inputs or nonpositive ratio denominators remain null.")
        sample["channels"].append(channel)

content.text:
## What the annotation pipeline does today

[`src/open_relief/annotation.py`](src/open_relief/annotation.py) is already fairly rigorous: strict Pydantic schema (`Claim`/`Annotation`), per-claim provenance tags (`observed` / `model_recalled` / `inference` — `retrieved` is explicitly disabled), cached+budget-guarded OpenAI calls, and hard leakage checks (a claim can't reference a month outside the input window, and the objective `phase` label can never be overwritten by the LLM). Good foundation.

But only **6 of 9,065 training examples have been annotated** ([`artifacts/annotations-final-pilot.jsonl`](artifacts/annotations-final-pilot.jsonl)) — the full run was deliberately deferred (per [`docs/PLAN.md`](docs/PLAN.md)). Looking at that pilot output, the claims are organized **per data source** (IPC chronology, then price, then FCS/rCSI) rather than as explicit cross-source interaction hypotheses. That's the core gap relative to what you want: a model that learns *port imports fell + conflict rose + rainfall dropped, together compounding into a phase-3 outcome*, not three separate factual notes.

## Evidence already in the repo that's relevant

The classical-baseline ablation ([`artifacts/ablations/metrics.json`](artifacts/ablations/metrics.json)) is worth knowing before deciding priorities:

| Features removed | Macro-F1 |
|---|---:|
| All sources | 0.5844 |
| Food history only (no shipping/conflict/rain/price) | **0.6032** |
| Without conflict | 0.5113 (biggest drop) |
| Without rainfall | 0.5615 |
| Without shipping | 0.5927 |
| Without prices | 0.6104 |

Naively stacking all channels into a *linear* model actually hurts it — food-history-only wins. Conflict and rainfall are the two channels that matter most individually. This is a good argument for OpenTSLM specifically (a nonlinear model with reasoning supervision might extract the interaction signal a linear model can't), and it tells us where to focus interaction-reasoning effort: conflict × rainfall × price combinations, not shipping.

## Gaps specific to "learn complex interactions"

1. **Schema/prompt reward per-channel facts, not cross-domain mechanisms.** No field currently forces the annotator to connect ≥2 different-source channels into one hypothesis.
2. **No retrieval grounding.** `model_recalled` is pure parametric memory; `validate_annotation` raises on any `retrieved` claim. `task.md` explicitly allows retrieval for important/uncertain claims — that's built into the spec but not implemented.
3. **Zero training-scale coverage.** Can't teach interaction reasoning at all until the full pass runs.
4. **No held-out explanation evaluation.** `task.md` §16 wants explanation quality judged separately from prediction accuracy; there's no ground truth for that on validation/test yet.
5. **SP vs. Flamingo undecided.** With 21 channels × 2 series (value+mask) = 42 series per example, the paper flags SP as scaling poorly with series count — directly relevant to whether the model can actually attend across many interacting signals.

## Proposed plan

**Must have**
1. Extend the `Claim`/`Annotation` schema + system prompt in `annotation.py` to require at least one explicit cross-domain interaction claim per example — naming ≥2 channels from different sources, a plausible mechanism, `provenance="inference"`, and a mandatory correlation-≠-causation hedge (small, contained code change).
2. Re-run the $2 mini pilot (`scripts/annotate_local.sh pilot`) offline-cache-style to sanity-check the new schema before spending real money.
3. Run the full annotation pass (`scripts/annotate_local.sh full`) — real OpenAI spend. Note: scaling the pilot's actual cost (~$0.0208/example) to 9,065 examples ≈ **$189**, right at the script's `--budget-usd 185` ceiling — I'd bump it to 190 (the code's hard cap) to avoid stopping short of full coverage.

**Should have**
4. Lightweight retrieval (ReliefWeb API / FEWS NET key messages / EM-DAT — all free, no auth) for country-months near a phase change, to ground "important/uncertain" claims with a real `source_url` and re-enable `retrieved` provenance instead of relying only on parametric recall.
5. A small held-out "explanation eval" set: annotate a fixed validation sample (never fed to the model as input) purely to score whether the fine-tuned model's generated rationale matches real precursor patterns.
6. Run the SP-vs-Flamingo comparison `train_gpu.py` already supports, given the many-channel scaling concern above.

**Nice to have**
7. An automated rationale "faithfulness" checker — verify a generated rationale's cited directions/magnitudes against the true numeric series, without a second paid annotation pass.
8. Two-way ablations (e.g., conflict+rainfall removed together) to check for super-/sub-additive effects and better target the interaction prompt.

Before I touch anything: the full annotation run spends real OpenAI money (~$185–190), and the retrieval idea adds a new external dependency. Want me to go ahead?

questions.question: Which of these should I start on right now?

options.label: Schema fix + full annotation run (Recommended)
options.description: Implement the cross-domain interaction claim requirement in annotation.py, sanity-check with the $2 pilot, then run the full ~$185-190 training-set annotation pass.

options.label: Schema fix only, hold off on spending
options.description: Implement and pilot-test the interaction-claim schema change, but don't run the full paid annotation pass yet — I'll ask again before spending.

options.label: Everything, including retrieval grounding
options.description: Also build the ReliefWeb/FEWS NET/EM-DAT retrieval step now, before running the full annotation pass, so retrieved evidence is included from the start.

## Done — schema change implemented, no money spent

Changes to [`src/open_relief/annotation.py`](src/open_relief/annotation.py):

- New `InteractionClaim` model (required, one per annotation, `min` enforced in code not schema): `provenance` restricted to `model_recalled`/`inference` (never `observed` — combining signals is analysis, not a raw reading), plus a `mechanism` field distinct from `statement` to force an explicit compounding explanation.
- `Annotation.interaction_hypotheses: list[InteractionClaim]` is now a required field alongside the existing `precursor_patterns`.
- `channel_domain()` maps channel names to real-world domains (`shipping_trade`, `conflict`, `rainfall`, `price`, `food_consumption`, `coping_behavior`, `food_security_assessment`, `calendar`) using the same prefix convention already used elsewhere in the codebase (`derived.py`, `adapter.py`).
- `validate_annotation` now rejects an annotation with zero interaction hypotheses, or one whose channels don't span **≥2 distinct domains** — so "conflict rose and price rose" passes, "conflict rose and conflict fatalities rose" doesn't.

"""Quantitative IPC scoring independent of explanation quality."""
import argparse
from collections import Counter
import json
from pathlib import Path
from .dataset import load_examples


def parse_prediction(text: str) -> dict | None:
    try:
        value = json.loads(text.strip().removeprefix('```json').removesuffix('```').strip())
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        return None
    if not isinstance(value, dict) or type(value.get("phase")) is not int or value["phase"] not in range(1, 6):
        return None
    if not isinstance(value.get("rationale"), str):
        return None
    return value


def score(rows: list[dict]) -> dict:
    from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score, recall_score, cohen_kappa_score
    if not rows:
        raise ValueError("Cannot score empty predictions")
    truth = [r["true_phase"] for r in rows]
    pred = [r["predicted_phase"] if r["predicted_phase"] in range(1, 6) else 0 for r in rows]
    valid = [i for i, p in enumerate(pred) if p != 0]
    result = {"n": len(rows), "accuracy": accuracy_score(truth, pred),
        "macro_f1_present_classes": f1_score(truth, pred, labels=sorted(set(truth)), average="macro", zero_division=0),
        "macro_f1_all_five": f1_score(truth, pred, labels=[1,2,3,4,5], average="macro", zero_division=0),
        "phase_recall": dict(zip(map(str, range(1,6)), recall_score(truth,pred,labels=[1,2,3,4,5],average=None,zero_division=0).tolist())),
        "invalid_rate": 1-len(valid)/len(rows),
        "ordinal_mae_valid_only": sum(abs(truth[i]-pred[i]) for i in valid)/len(valid) if valid else None}
    eligible = [r for r in rows if r.get("baseline_phase") is not None]
    if eligible:
        y = [r["true_phase"] > r["baseline_phase"] for r in eligible]
        p = [r["predicted_phase"] > r["baseline_phase"] if r["predicted_phase"] else False for r in eligible]
        result["secondary_deterioration"] = {"n": len(y), "f1": f1_score(y,p,zero_division=0),
            "recall": recall_score(y,p,zero_division=0),
            "definition": "Any phase increase over available assessment; invalid predictions count as no alert."}

content.text:
## What goes TO the LLM annotator (`request_payload`, `annotation.py`)

One request = system prompt + one JSON user message. Sent for **train split only**, never val/test.

System prompt: rules. Copy `phase` label, never relabel. Distinguish `observed`/`model_recalled`/`inference`, no `retrieved` (no retrieval tool wired up). Numeric-only claims on FCS/rCSI (normalization unknown). ≥1 cross-domain `interaction_hypotheses` required.

User message = plain JSON, real numbers, e.g. this example (Hajr, Yemen, cutoff 2020-07):
```json
"input": {
  "geography": {...}, "cutoff": "2020-07-31T23:59:59Z", "horizon_months": 3,
  "last_available_phase": {"phase": 2, "event_month": "2020-06", "age_months_at_cutoff": 1},
  "channels": [ {"name": "portwatch_import_cargo", "months": [...6 months...], "values": [688563, 713090, 770018, 675759, 629638, 881028]}, ...21 channels ],
  "ipc_assessment_timeline": [...]
},
"target": {"phase": 3, "phase_change": 1, "deteriorated": true, "target_month": "2020-10"}
```

Key point: **`target.phase = 3` (the future outcome) is sent to the annotator.** That's allowed — annotator explains history *given* known outcome. Model never sees this at inference; only training supervision sees it.

## What comes BACK

One JSON object, validated against strict schema (`Annotation`):
- `observed_future_phase`: must equal `target.phase` exactly (3) — code rejects any mismatch
- `precursor_patterns`: per-channel facts ("conflict events 787→962", "cargo -12.5% vs 3mo avg")
- `interaction_hypotheses`: ≥1 cross-domain claim ("conflict peak + import shortfall → jointly plausible pressure on cost/access"), `provenance: inference`, always hedged
- `rationale`: short paragraph, this is what actually gets used downstream
- `confidence`: 0.72 here

Every claim checked in Python: channels must exist, months must be inside input window (or the known target month), no fabricated URLs, interaction claims must span ≥2 real domains.

## One final training data point (what OpenTSLM actually trains on)

Built by `format_training()` (`adapter.py`) from dataset example + annotation. **Note: annotation's `target.phase`/future context is stripped out here** — only `rationale` text survives into training.

```
pre_prompt: "Forecast FEWS NET IPC phase 3 months after cutoff 2020-07-31...
             District: Hajr, Hadramawt, Yemen... Last available IPC assessment:
             {phase:2, event_month:2020-06}."
time_series: [42 series]   # 21 channels × (value series + observed-mask series)
time_series_text: [42 descriptions]  # one description string per series above
post_prompt: "Prediction JSON:"
answer: '{"phase": 3, "rationale": "Observed ground truth is Phase 3... conflict
          intensity elevated March-May, price rose May, cargo fell April-May
          before recovering June..."}'
```

Model sees: numbers + text description of channels + prompt. Model does NOT see: `target.phase`, `interaction_hypotheses`, `confidence`, or any future month data (`format_input`/`format_training` hard-reject any value whose `availability_time` is after cutoff — that's the leakage guard).

## How improvement gets measured later (`gpu.py`, `evaluate.py`)

Same held-out test cohort (2,230 examples, Aug-Dec 2023 cutoffs), evaluated twice with identical code path:

1. **Pretrained OpenTSLM** (no Open Relief training) → `model.generate()` on `format_input()` only (no answer given) → parse JSON → score.
2. **Open Relief fine-tuned** (same checkpoint, LoRA-tuned on the annotated train set) → same eval loop.

`score()` in `evaluate.py` computes, both times, on the identical test set:
- `accuracy`, `macro_f1_present_classes`, `macro_f1_all_five`
- `phase_recall` per class 1-5
- `invalid_rate` (model output didn't parse as valid phase 1-5)
- `ordinal_mae_valid_only` (how far off, not just right/wrong)
- `secondary_deterioration.f1`/`.recall` — did it flag a phase increase over last known assessment (this is the one where a persistence baseline currently scores 0 recall despite 0.735 macro-F1 — the real bar to beat)
- per-country breakdown

`gpu.py` writes both runs' rows/metrics + a `benchmark.md` table (Pretrained vs Open Relief, Macro-F1/Accuracy/Invalid rate) automatically. That table is the actual "did fine-tuning help" answer — nothing claimed until it runs.
